screens.title: Database per Service Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore the Database per Service pattern, a core practice when moving from a monolith to microservices. Rather than a single shared database, each microservice owns its private data store. This gives teams full control over schema, migrations, and even the database technology they choose, enabling faster independent deployments and resilience when a single data store fails. You'll see why this increases autonomy but also why it forces a shift from immediate, cross-service ACID transactions to designs that accept eventual consistency and rely on APIs or domain events. We'll ground these ideas with a practical hands-on plan to build a simple ProductService using an embedded H2 database and REST APIs. You'll also learn the common beginner mistake of directly querying another service's database and why that breaks encapsulation. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the trade-offs, pick appropriate integration strategies, and start a small service with its own datastore. Think about what data your service truly owns; that ownership determines the boundaries you will protect.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Database per Service Pattern
Database per Service Pattern
Own your data, free your teams — and plan for distributed consistency
What you will understand
Why per-service databases improve autonomy, the consistency trade-offs, and practical ways to integrate services safely.
Why it matters
Services can evolve independently, choose the best storage for their data, and avoid team bottlenecks tied to a shared schema.
Explore Key Topics
Autonomy
Teams control schema and migrations without cross-service coordination.
Consistency
Accept eventual consistency and design event-driven updates or sagas.
Hands-on
Build a ProductService with its own H2 database and REST endpoints.
System sketch
Shared database (anti-pattern)
Users, Orders and Products tables live in one DB. Schema changes affect all teams and create a coupling point.
Database per Service
UserService → users_db, OrderService → orders_db, ProductService → products_db. Services communicate by API or events.
Note
Do not directly query another service's database. Use the owning service's API or published events to request or subscribe to data changes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over these two objective screens you'll see concrete, measurable skills to practice. First, you will explain why teams pick a dedicated database per microservice: you should be able to argue how separation removes a central coupling point and speeds independent deployments. Third, you'll analyze the practical challenges introduced by data fragmentation: why cross-service transactions are hard and how that leads to eventual consistency patterns. Fourth, you'll design strategies for maintaining data correctness across services, including using APIs, domain events, or higher-level patterns like sagas. Each objective pairs a clear task with why it matters in real teams, so you can assess whether you've internalized both the concept and its practical impact.

screens.title: Shared Database vs Database per Service
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare a shared database in a monolith with a database per service approach using a simple e-commerce example: Users, Products, and Orders. In a shared database model all tables live together. This gives you straightforward ACID transactions across tables, but it creates a single coupling point. Teams must coordinate schema migrations, run risk of cascading failures, and scale the database as the whole application grows. In contrast, database per service gives each service its own store: UserService owns users_db, ProductService owns products_db, and OrderService owns orders_db. This separation enables teams to choose different storage types and to deploy independently. However, you no longer have immediate cross-service ACID guarantees. For example, creating an order and decrementing inventory in another service cannot rely on a single atomic transaction. A common misconception is that splitting databases always increases complexity without benefit; in practice it trades centralized simplicity for team autonomy and resilience. The practical takeaway is to treat ownership as the decisive factor: if a service owns a piece of data, it should be the only process changing it. When other services need that data, they should request it through the owning service's A P I or subscribe to events rather than direct database reads. Which parts of your domain must remain strongly consistent and which can accept eventual consistency determines the right approach.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Shared vs Per-Service DB
Shared database (monolith)
Single store for Users, Products, Orders
Pros: easy ACID transactions and simple joins. Cons: schema coupling, migration coordination, single failure domain.
Concrete example
A single transaction updates Orders table and Products inventory in one atomic commit. Teams must coordinate migrations affecting both tables.
Common mistake
Relying on this pattern during a microservice migration reintroduces coupling and slows independent deployments.
Database per Service
Each service owns its own datastore
Pros: autonomy, polyglot choices, independent migrations. Cons: no cross-service ACID, requires integration patterns for consistency.
Concrete example
OrderService creates an order in orders_db and publishes OrderCreatedEvent. ProductService subscribes and decrements inventory in products_db.
Pro tip
Map ownership clearly: a service may replicate read-only copies of other data, but the owning service must remain authoritative for writes.
Key takeaway
Choose ownership boundaries first. Use shared DB only when team isolation is not a priority; otherwise plan integration patterns for per-service databases.

screens.title: What does 'Database per Service' mean?
screens.narratorSegment: Database per Service means each microservice is the sole owner and manager of its private data store. Ownership implies responsibility for schema, migrations, backup and restore, and the integrity of the data. A concrete example: a UserService owns the user records and authentication details; OrderService stores order history and statuses; ProductService keeps catalog data. Ownership also implies that other services must never reach into these databases directly. A frequent beginner error is to shortcut integration by querying another service's tables; doing so breaks encapsulation and makes upgrades brittle. Instead, consumers should request data through the owning service's A P I or keep a locally maintained, eventually consistent copy derived from domain events. Another aspect is polyglot persistence: services can pick the datastore that suits their access patterns. For instance, you might choose PostgreSQL for transactional order data, a document store for rapidly changing product catalogs, or a graph database where relationships are primary. The ownership rule is simple: the owning service handles writes and business rules; any other service treats that data as authoritative only via that service's interfaces or published events. End with the rule in mind: ownership defines control and evolution boundaries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Definition
Database per Service
Each microservice owns and manages a private data store and schema.
Concrete examples
  • OrderService → orders_db (relational for transactions)
  • ProductService → products_db (document store for flexible attributes)
  • UserService → users_db (relational with authentication data)
Ownership rule
Only the owning service writes its data. Others must use the owning service's API or subscribe to its domain events for updates.
Why ownership matters
Ownership protects the service's ability to change its schema and storage without coordinating across teams. It reduces coupling and lets services scale independently.
Misconception check
Some think owning a DB prevents read access; it does not. Read-only caches or API responses are acceptable. What is forbidden is direct writes or schema-dependent reads that bypass the owner.
Practical tip
Map each domain entity to an owning service before splitting databases. Misplaced ownership creates friction later.

screens.title: Managing consistency: eventual consistency and patterns
screens.narratorSegment: When data is split across databases you cannot rely on a single global ACID transaction for multi-service updates. Instead, architects commonly accept eventual consistency and use patterns to move data between services. The basic flow is: a service performs a local transaction and then emits a domain event describing the change. Other services subscribe and asynchronously update their own state or trigger side effects. For example, OrderService creates an order in orders_db and publishes OrderCreatedEvent. InventoryService consumes the event and decrements stock in products_db. This decouples services and avoids distributed two-phase commits. A common alternative is synchronous A P I calls: the calling service requests a synchronous read or action from the owning service. This preserves immediate consistency for that operation but ties services together and increases latency and availability coupling. Beginners sometimes conflate the two: synchronous calls are not the same as owning the data. If you need low-latency strong consistency for a specific operation, prefer the owning service's A P I. If you can tolerate short windows of inconsistency, publish domain events and accept eventual convergence. The takeaway is to choose the integration style by consistency needs: synchronous when correctness must be immediate, asynchronous when throughput and autonomy matter more.

keyIdea.title: Consistency approach
keyIdea.text: Use synchronous APIs for immediate needs; use domain events and eventual consistency for decoupling and scalability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Consistency Patterns
From local commit to system-wide consistency
Choose between immediate sync calls and asynchronous eventual consistency patterns.
Step 1: Local transaction
Service performs a local commit inside its own database and enforces local business rules.
Step 2: Publish domain event
Publish an event such as OrderCreatedEvent describing the change, for other services to consume asynchronously.
Step 3: Subscribers react
Interested services update their local state, trigger workflows, or send notifications, eventually converging the system.
When to use sync APIs
When correctness must be immediate and you can accept tighter coupling and latency sensitivity.
When to use events
When autonomy, scalability, and decoupling are more important and temporary inconsistency is acceptable.

screens.title: Domain Events: loosely coupled integration
screens.narratorSegment: Domain events are notifications emitted by a service when something significant happens within its domain. They are statements of fact, like OrderCreated or InventoryDecreased, not commands. Emitting an event after a successful local transaction allows other services to receive that information asynchronously and react. For example, after OrderService persists an order it publishes OrderCreatedEvent. PaymentService may subscribe to start payment processing; NotificationService may subscribe to send an email. Events decouple producers and consumers: the producer doesn't need to know how many subscribers there are or what they do. A common novice mistake is to overuse events for queries: events are best for informing about changes, not returning on-demand data. For immediate data needs, call the owning service synchronously. Another subtlety is that events need clear schemas and backward compatibility strategies to evolve safely. Also plan for failure cases: if a subscriber fails to process an event, you may need retry or dead-letter handling. In practice, domain events plus eventual consistency let systems scale and evolve independently while maintaining a loosely coupled communication surface. Domain Events: loosely coupled integration means emit facts about state changes to inform other services; use events for updates and apis for direct queries.. In practical terms, how events propagate state changes and examples from e-commerce. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Emit facts about state changes to inform other services; use events for updates and APIs for direct queries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Domain Events
What is a domain event?
A published notification that a significant state change occurred in a service, for other services to consume.
Example sequence
  1. OrderService saves order in orders_db.
  2. OrderService publishes OrderCreatedEvent.
  3. InventoryService consumes event, decrements stock in products_db.
Misconception
Events are not a substitute for on-demand reads. Use the owning service's API for immediate queries.
Operational concerns
Define event schemas, versioning, retry behavior, and dead-letter handling so subscribers can process reliably.
Practical tip
Keep events small and explicit about intent. Avoid embedding large payloads; include references that subscribers can fetch if needed.
Key takeaway
Domain events enable asynchronous, resilient communication when ownership boundaries prevent direct shared writes.

screens.title: Saga patterns and long-running transactions (overview)
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed transactions that touch multiple databases often tempt teams to look for two-phase commit solutions. In practice two-phase commits tie availability and performance to a coordinator and are seldom used across microservices. Instead, the Saga pattern decomposes a long-running business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each controlled by a single service. If one step fails, the saga triggers compensating transactions that undo earlier steps. For example, creating an order might include local steps: reserve inventory, charge payment, confirm order. If the payment fails after inventory was reserved, a compensating action releases the reserved inventory. There are two basic saga styles: choreography, where services emit and react to events to drive the saga, and orchestration, where a coordinator service directs each step. A common misconception is that sagas automatically guarantee immediate consistency; they instead provide controlled eventual consistency with explicit failure handling. When designing sagas, define clear compensating actions and ensure idempotency of steps since retries will occur. The practical trade-off is explicit complexity in business logic for higher availability and independence of services. Saga patterns and long-running transactions (overview) means break a distributed transaction into local steps with compensating actions to handle failure and preserve eventual consistency.. In practical terms, why two-phase commits are avoided and how sagas help. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Saga Patterns
Sagas for long-running transactions
Sequence local transactions and compensations instead of distributed atomic commits.
Choreography
Services publish events and other services react. No central coordinator. Good for simple sagas where steps map naturally to events.
Orchestration
A dedicated orchestrator tells services which local transaction to run next. Easier to reason about complex flows but introduces a coordinator component.
Design checklist
  • Define local transactions and compensating actions
  • Ensure idempotency and retry behavior
  • Prefer eventual consistency where acceptable

screens.title: Anti-patterns: direct DB access and shared schemas
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent anti-pattern is direct access to another service's database. Teams do this to avoid the latency or complexity of A P I calls, but it reintroduces tight coupling. Direct queries make the caller dependent on the owner's schema and migrations; a change by the owning team can silently break multiple consumers. Another anti-pattern is creating shared tables that multiple services write to. Shared writes defeat the purpose of ownership and make it impossible for a single service to evolve its schema independently. Instead, use the owning service's A P I for synchronous needs, or subscribe to events for asynchronous updates. If performance demands local reads, maintain a local read replica or cache that is populated via events, but treat it as eventually consistent and read-only for the data that is owned elsewhere. When you see a pull to query another DB, ask whether the immediate benefit outweighs the long-term costs of coupling. The practical enforcement is organizational as much as technical: document ownership, enforce team boundaries, and review integrations in architecture reviews to catch accidental direct DB access. Anti-patterns: direct DB access and shared schemas means never query another service's database for writes or schema-dependent reads; prefer apis, events, or local read replicas.. In practical terms, why bypassing service apis breaks ownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Never query another service's database for writes or schema-dependent reads; prefer APIs, events, or local read replicas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Anti-patterns
Direct DB access
Problem: Consumers become dependent on internal schema, causing brittle integrations and coordination bottlenecks.
Safe alternative
Call the owning service's API or subscribe to its events to get a copy of the data instead of querying its tables.
Shared writable tables
Problem: Multiple services writing the same tables break ownership and complicate migrations and scaling.
Safe alternative
Keep writes encapsulated and use events to propagate state changes to other services for local read models.
Checklist
  • Can the owning service provide an API for this need?
  • Would an event-driven copy satisfy the latency and correctness needs?
  • If local reads are required, can they be eventual and read-only?

screens.title: Implementing ProductService — entity and repository
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through the hands-on ProductService implementation. The Product entity models the data owned by ProductService: id, name, description, and price. The entity is a straightforward JPA-managed class. The repository is a simple JpaRepository that gives you CRUD operations without explicit S Q L. Together they demonstrate how a service controls its own schema and persistence mechanics. A concrete example: when you add a new product with the repository's save method, the change is localized to products_db and any migrations only affect this service. A common misconception is that this code somehow prevents other services from reading product data. It doesn't; you still expose read endpoints or publish events, but other teams must not directly modify or depend on the internal schema. Study the code to see how the entity fields map to columns and how the repository abstracts CRUD operations. After this you will see the controller and configuration for H2 and example curl requests to exercise the endpoints. package com.cohortia.productservice.model;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

@Entity
public class Product {
  @Id
  @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
  private Long id;
  private String name;
  private String description;
  private BigDecimal price;

  public Product() {}

  public Product(String name, String description, BigDecimal price) {
    this.name = name;
    this.description = description;
    this.price = price;
  }

  // Getters and setters omitted for brevity
}

public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › ProductController & Demo
ProductController outline
<!-- ProductController.java -->
package com.cohortia.productservice.controller;

import com.cohortia.productservice.model.Product;
import com.cohortia.productservice.repository.ProductRepository;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/products")
public class ProductController {
  private final ProductRepository repo;
  public ProductController(ProductRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

  @PostMapping
  public Product create(@RequestBody Product p) { return repo.save(p); }

  @GetMapping("/{id}")
  public Product get(@PathVariable Long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElse(null); }

  @PutMapping("/{id}")
  public Product update(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Product p) {
    p.setId(id);
    return repo.save(p);
  }
}
application.properties (H2)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:productdb
spring.datasource.driverClassName=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
spring.h2.console.enabled=true
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
Terminal demo
# Create a product
curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Lamp","description":"Desk lamp","price":19.99}' http://localhost:8080/products

# Retrieve the created product
curl -s http://localhost:8080/products/1
These commands create and read product data in ProductService's private H2 database. They demonstrate ownership and local persistence.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore the Database per Service pattern, a core practice when moving from a monolith to microservices. Rather than a single shared database, each microservice owns its private data store. This gives teams full control over schema, migrations, and even the database technology they choose, enabling faster independent deployments and resilience when a single data store fails. You'll see why this increases autonomy but also why it forces a shift from immediate, cross-service ACID transactions to designs that accept eventual consistency and rely on APIs or domain events. We'll ground these ideas with a practical hands-on plan to build a simple ProductService using an embedded H2 database and REST APIs. You'll also learn the common beginner mistake of directly querying another service's database and why that breaks encapsulation. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the trade-offs, pick appropriate integration strategies, and start a small service with its own datastore. Think about what data your service truly owns; that ownership determines the boundaries you will protect.

Over these two objective screens you'll see concrete, measurable skills to practice. First, you will explain why teams pick a dedicated database per microservice: you should be able to argue how separation removes a central coupling point and speeds independent deployments. Second, you will identify the main benefits such as service autonomy and the ability to choose different databases — often called polyglot persistence — and be ready to give examples when relational or document stores are preferable. Third, you'll analyze the practical challenges introduced by data fragmentation: why cross-service transactions are hard and how that leads to eventual consistency patterns. Fourth, you'll design strategies for maintaining data correctness across services, including using APIs, domain events, or higher-level patterns like sagas. Each objective pairs a clear task with why it matters in real teams, so you can assess whether you've internalized both the concept and its practical impact.

On this second objectives screen we'll focus on practical and implementation skills. You will implement a basic ProductService with a dedicated H2 datastore, REST endpoints, and repository wiring. That means you can scaffold the Spring Boot project, define the Product entity, create a JpaRepository, and expose create, read, and update endpoints. Next, you'll test the service using curl or Postman to prove it runs independently and that schema changes are local to the service. Another objective is to evaluate anti-patterns: you'll be able to explain why directly querying another service's database is harmful and what to do instead. Finally, you'll practice choosing between synchronous A P I calls and asynchronous events for integration and know the consequences for consistency and latency. Each objective maps to a small demo or discussion so you can validate competency by running the starter code and executing sample requests.

Let's compare a shared database in a monolith with a database per service approach using a simple e-commerce example: Users, Products, and Orders. In a shared database model all tables live together. This gives you straightforward ACID transactions across tables, but it creates a single coupling point. Teams must coordinate schema migrations, run risk of cascading failures, and scale the database as the whole application grows. In contrast, database per service gives each service its own store: UserService owns users_db, ProductService owns products_db, and OrderService owns orders_db. This separation enables teams to choose different storage types and to deploy independently. However, you no longer have immediate cross-service ACID guarantees. For example, creating an order and decrementing inventory in another service cannot rely on a single atomic transaction. A common misconception is that splitting databases always increases complexity without benefit; in practice it trades centralized simplicity for team autonomy and resilience. The practical takeaway is to treat ownership as the decisive factor: if a service owns a piece of data, it should be the only process changing it. When other services need that data, they should request it through the owning service's A P I or subscribe to events rather than direct database reads. Which parts of your domain must remain strongly consistent and which can accept eventual consistency determines the right approach.

Database per Service means each microservice is the sole owner and manager of its private data store. Ownership implies responsibility for schema, migrations, backup and restore, and the integrity of the data. A concrete example: a UserService owns the user records and authentication details; OrderService stores order history and statuses; ProductService keeps catalog data. Ownership also implies that other services must never reach into these databases directly. A frequent beginner error is to shortcut integration by querying another service's tables; doing so breaks encapsulation and makes upgrades brittle. Instead, consumers should request data through the owning service's A P I or keep a locally maintained, eventually consistent copy derived from domain events. Another aspect is polyglot persistence: services can pick the datastore that suits their access patterns. For instance, you might choose PostgreSQL for transactional order data, a document store for rapidly changing product catalogs, or a graph database where relationships are primary. The ownership rule is simple: the owning service handles writes and business rules; any other service treats that data as authoritative only via that service's interfaces or published events. End with the rule in mind: ownership defines control and evolution boundaries.

When data is split across databases you cannot rely on a single global ACID transaction for multi-service updates. Instead, architects commonly accept eventual consistency and use patterns to move data between services. The basic flow is: a service performs a local transaction and then emits a domain event describing the change. Other services subscribe and asynchronously update their own state or trigger side effects. For example, OrderService creates an order in orders_db and publishes OrderCreatedEvent. InventoryService consumes the event and decrements stock in products_db. This decouples services and avoids distributed two-phase commits. A common alternative is synchronous A P I calls: the calling service requests a synchronous read or action from the owning service. This preserves immediate consistency for that operation but ties services together and increases latency and availability coupling. Beginners sometimes conflate the two: synchronous calls are not the same as owning the data. If you need low-latency strong consistency for a specific operation, prefer the owning service's A P I. If you can tolerate short windows of inconsistency, publish domain events and accept eventual convergence. The takeaway is to choose the integration style by consistency needs: synchronous when correctness must be immediate, asynchronous when throughput and autonomy matter more.

Domain events are notifications emitted by a service when something significant happens within its domain. They are statements of fact, like OrderCreated or InventoryDecreased, not commands. Emitting an event after a successful local transaction allows other services to receive that information asynchronously and react. For example, after OrderService persists an order it publishes OrderCreatedEvent. PaymentService may subscribe to start payment processing; NotificationService may subscribe to send an email. Events decouple producers and consumers: the producer doesn't need to know how many subscribers there are or what they do. A common novice mistake is to overuse events for queries: events are best for informing about changes, not returning on-demand data. For immediate data needs, call the owning service synchronously. Another subtlety is that events need clear schemas and backward compatibility strategies to evolve safely. Also plan for failure cases: if a subscriber fails to process an event, you may need retry or dead-letter handling. In practice, domain events plus eventual consistency let systems scale and evolve independently while maintaining a loosely coupled communication surface. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Distributed transactions that touch multiple databases often tempt teams to look for two-phase commit solutions. In practice two-phase commits tie availability and performance to a coordinator and are seldom used across microservices. Instead, the Saga pattern decomposes a long-running business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each controlled by a single service. If one step fails, the saga triggers compensating transactions that undo earlier steps. For example, creating an order might include local steps: reserve inventory, charge payment, confirm order. If the payment fails after inventory was reserved, a compensating action releases the reserved inventory. There are two basic saga styles: choreography, where services emit and react to events to drive the saga, and orchestration, where a coordinator service directs each step. A common misconception is that sagas automatically guarantee immediate consistency; they instead provide controlled eventual consistency with explicit failure handling. When designing sagas, define clear compensating actions and ensure idempotency of steps since retries will occur. The practical trade-off is explicit complexity in business logic for higher availability and independence of services. A frequent anti-pattern is direct access to another service's database. Teams do this to avoid the latency or complexity of A P I calls, but it reintroduces tight coupling. Direct queries make the caller dependent on the owner's schema and migrations; a change by the owning team can silently break multiple consumers. Another anti-pattern is creating shared tables that multiple services write to. Shared writes defeat the purpose of ownership and make it impossible for a single service to evolve its schema independently. Instead, use the owning service's A P I for synchronous needs, or subscribe to events for asynchronous updates. If performance demands local reads, maintain a local read replica or cache that is populated via events, but treat it as eventually consistent and read-only for the data that is owned elsewhere. When you see a pull to query another DB, ask whether the immediate benefit outweighs the long-term costs of coupling. A final set of core ideas to keep: Eventual Consistency describes the acceptance that replicas or derived data will converge over time and that systems relying on domain events must tolerate short-term inconsistency. Domain Events are the mechanism services use to notify others about state changes without sharing a database. Distributed Transactions are those that span multiple services; instead of two-phase commit, architects often use sagas to sequence local transactions with compensations on failure. When designing systems, weigh whether a business operation requires immediate consistency or can tolerate eventual convergence. That decision drives whether you call an A P I synchronously or publish an event asynchronously. Keep this question central as you apply the Database per Service pattern in real projects. Key Concepts means choose sync apis for immediate consistency, events and sagas for distributed workflows and higher autonomy with eventual consistency..
